{{smaller block|The oval ''tool-stones'', . . . or "Tilhuggersteens" of the northern antiquaries, are oval or egg-shaped stones, more or less indented on one or both surfaces. {{smaller block|Before a craftsman can recognise a ''tool-mark'', he must be familiar with the tool; before a geologist knows river-marks, he must study the ways of rivers.

'''tool-marking''' (töl′mär″king), ''n.'' A method of etching marks or names on steel tools, consisting in coating the part to be marked thinly with tallow or beeswax, making the desired marking with a sharp-pointed instrument through this coating, and applying nitric acid. {{smaller|After a few minutes, the acid and tallow are washed off, and the marks are found to show clearly on the steel.}}

'''tool-post''' (töl′pōst), ''n.'' In a lathe, a holder or support for the cutting-tool. {{smaller|It consists of an upright piece on the slide-rest, fitted with a slot through which the cutting-tool is passed, and a set-screw for holding the tool in position. Also ''tool-stock''.}}

'''tool-rest''' (töl′rest), ''n.'' A device on the front of a lathe, used either as a support for a hand-tool or for holding a cutting-tool in position. It has sometimes various adjustments for moving the tool. See ''slide-rest'', and cut under ''lathe''.

{{smaller block|Tho' perhaps he had never a Shirt to his Back, yet he would have a ''toting'' huge swelling Ruff about his Neck.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. iii. 32.}}}}

2. To shoot up, as plants. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—3†. To become visible; peep out; show.

{{smaller block|His hod was full of holes & his heer oute,
With his knopped schon clouted ful thykke;
His ton [toes] ''toteden'' out as he the londe treddede.
{{right|''Piers Plowman's Crede'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 425.}}}}

4†. To glance; peer; look; gaze; pore.

{{smaller block|Tristly may Troiell ''tote'' ouer the walle,
And loke vpon lenght, er his loue come!
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 8178.}}}}

{{smaller block|How fair Narcissus, ''tooting'' on his shade,
Reproves disdain, and tells how form doth vade.
{{right|''Peele'', Arraignment of Paris, i. 5.}}}}

5. Hence, to look or search narrowly; pry inquisitively. [Obsolete or prov. Eng.]

{{smaller block|Those observants were spying, ''tooting'', and looking, watching and prying, what they might hear or see against the see of Rome.
{{right|''Latimer'', Misc. Selections.}}}}

{{smaller block|Nor ''toot'' in Cheapside baskets earne and late.
{{right|''Bp. Hall'', Satires, IV. ii. 45.}}}}

6. To try; endeavor. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''II.'''† ''trans.'' To see; behold; observe.

{{smaller block|Whow myʒt-tou in thine brother eiʒe a bare mote loken,
And in thyn owen eiʒe nouʒt a bem ''toten?''
{{right|''Piers Plowman's Crede'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 142.}}}}
